On December 23, 2024, President Biden commuted the sentences of 37 of the 40 prisoners on federal death row, converting them to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole and leaving only three "hard cases" before Donald Trump's January 20 inauguration.[n] Biden said he was "more convinced than ever that we must stop the use of the death penalty at the federal level," and framed the action as consistent with his administration's moratorium on federal executions "in cases other than terrorism and hate-motivated mass murder."[n] He added that he condemned the murderers, grieved for the victims, and ached for the families who had suffered "unimaginable and irreparable loss."[n] The three excluded inmates were two mass shooters and the Boston Marathon bomber.[n] The action followed a weeks-long pressure campaign by [[amnesty-international|Amnesty International]] and allied NGOs, partly premised on the argument that the federal death penalty is applied in a racially discriminatory manner.[n] Badlands commentator Ashe in America questioned whether "illegitimate presidents have pardon powers," suggesting only Biden's Thanksgiving turkey pardons would survive a genuine truth-and-reconciliation process.[n] The episode is covered in detail at [[2024-federal-death-row-commutations]].[n]

In a Truth Social post on Monday, December 23, 2024, President-elect Trump revived the proposal that the United States take control of [[greenland|Greenland]], declaring that "for purposes of National Security and Freedom throughout the World, the United States of America feels that the ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity."[n] The statement accompanied his nomination of PayPal cofounder [[ken-howery|Ken Howery]] as U.S. Ambassador to [[denmark|Denmark]], the NATO ally of which Greenland is an autonomous territory.[n] Earlier the same day Trump attacked the fees charged for use of the [[panama-canal|Panama Canal]], writing that "the fees being charged by Panama are ridiculous, especially knowing the extraordinary generosity that has been bestowed to Panama by the U.S.," calling it a complete "rip-off" and warning that if Panama failed to observe "moral and legal principles" the United States would demand full control of the canal, adding: "To the Officials of Panama, please be guided accordingly!"[n] Badlands analyst Burning Bright read the posts as deliberate signal rather than trolling, noting that the Panama deployment tracked the same memetic and media structure as Trump's earlier Canada messaging — which, he argued, prompted near-immediate capitulation from Justin Trudeau and the apparent collapse of the government in Ottawa — and that his tariff threats against Claudia Sheinbaum preceded Mexico's largest fentanyl bust in years.[n] The effect, Burning Bright wrote, was to push global conversation toward the [[monroe-doctrine|Monroe Doctrine]] and the Panama Papers, and to raise the question of why relatively small European powers control vast distant land masses.[n]

In December 2024, CBS News aired a 60 Minutes segment in which two recently retired senior Mossad officers, identified only as "Michael" and "Gabriel" and appearing masked with altered voices, described their leading roles in the September 17 pager plot against [[hezbollah|Hezbollah]].[n] The report characterized the operation as one of the most daring and sophisticated deceptions in the history of counterintelligence — a modern Trojan horse in which Mossad "created a bomb in a pocket" and tricked Hezbollah fighters into wearing the devices on their bodies.[n] The segment credited the plot's repercussions with aiding the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, weakening Iran, and decimating Hezbollah.[n] The officers said Mossad activated dormant walkie-talkies the following day, some detonating at funerals of those killed by the pagers; roughly 30 people died, including two children, and about 3,000 were injured.[n] "Gabriel" stated that the aim was not simply to kill: wounded fighters require hospitals, money, and effort, and "those people without hands and eyes are living proof, walking in Lebanon, of 'don't mess with us.'"[n] The segment described Mossad's motto, from Proverbs 24:6, as endorsing war through deception and trickery, likened to the [[central-intelligence-agency|CIA]]'s "smoke and mirrors"; former Mossad officer [[victor-ostrovsky|Victor Ostrovsky]], author of the whistleblower book By Way of Deception, has said the agency's original motto was "By way of deception, thou shalt do war."[n] Badlands commentator GhostofBasedPatrickHenry speculated the interviews might be a "Ghosts in the Machine" deployment designed to humiliate Mossad, noting that Bibi Netanyahu, David Barnea, Israel Katz, or other Israeli officials could have disavowed the commentary, and concluded that the officers came across as "uncivilized savages" who embodied everything they accuse their enemies of being.[n]
60 Minutes Account of the Pager Plot

In a December 2024 CBS News 60 Minutes segment, two retired senior [[mossad|Mossad]] officers detailed how the Israeli service built and sold booby-trapped pagers to Hezbollah fighters, detonating them on September 17 after nearly a year of escalating war between Israel and the organization.[n] The officers said Mossad activated long-dormant walkie-talkies the following day, some exploding at funerals for those killed by the pagers, with roughly 30 people killed, including two children, and about 3,000 injured.[n] One officer explained that maiming rather than killing was the objective, since wounded survivors "without hands and eyes" would serve as walking proof of Israeli superiority across the Middle East.[n] CBS reported that the plot's repercussions included aiding the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, weakening Iran, and decimating Hezbollah itself.[n]

A December 2024 Daily Mail report highlighted a CIA document, 'Mars Exploration May 22, 1984,' which describes the agency using astral projection to transport a 'subject' to Mars approximately one million years BC.[n] The subject reported an "oblique view of a pyramid" and a "very large road" with a monument resembling those of ancient Egypt, and described a population of "very large people" searching for "a new place to live because their environment was corrupted."[n] The study was part of [[project-stargate|Project Stargate]], the secret US Army unit established in 1977 at [[fort-meade|Fort Meade]], Maryland, that studied remote viewing, telepathy, and psychokinesis.[n] Badlands commentator GhostofBasedPatrickHenry asked whether the CIA was "pulling our leg" or whether the disclosure represented signal from Ghosts in the Machine.[n]
CIA Mars Document and Fort Meade Context

A CIA report titled 'Mars Exploration May 22, 1984,' surfaced in December 2024 reporting, details the use of astral projection — the idea that a person's spirit can travel through the astral plane — to transport a 'subject' to Mars approximately one million years BC.[n] The subject described an oblique view of a pyramid, a very large road, and a monument resembling ancient Egyptian works, then a population of "very large people" seeking a new home because their environment had been corrupted.[n] Participants in the program were exposed to binaural beats and hemi-sync audio to induce altered states of consciousness and promote psychic abilities.[n] Established in 1977 as a secret US Army unit, Stargate was framed as a weapon against the Soviet Union aimed at creating mind-reading spies able to infiltrate enemy minds, and was conducted at [[fort-meade|Fort Meade]] in Maryland, recruiting men and women who claimed extrasensory perception.[n] The program shut down in 1995; over its more than ten-year existence, psychics known as "remote viewers" participated in operations ranging from locating hostages kidnapped by Islamic terrorist groups to tracing fugitives inside the United States.[n] Badlands commentary noted the resemblance of this description to the plot of the Netflix series Stranger Things.[n]

On December 23, 2024, President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] revived proposals for U.S. control of Greenland, posting on Truth Social that "for purposes of National Security and Freedom throughout the World, the United States of America feels that the ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity."[n] The statement was made as part of his announcement nominating PayPal cofounder [[ken-howery|Ken Howery]] as U.S. Ambassador to [[denmark|Denmark]].[n] Greenland, the world's largest island, is an autonomous territory of Denmark, a key U.S. ally and NATO member.[n] Badlands analyst Burning Bright framed the post as signal, asking whether Trump was drawing attention to the relationship between relatively minor European powers and the enormous land masses they control.[n]

Hours before reviving his [[greenland|Greenland]] proposal on December 23, 2024, President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] criticized the fees charged for use of the Panama Canal, writing that "the fees being charged by Panama are ridiculous, especially knowing the extraordinary generosity that has been bestowed to Panama by the U.S."[n] He called the situation a complete "rip-off" and warned that if Panama failed to comply with what he described as "moral and legal principles," the United States would demand full control of the canal, closing with "To the Officials of Panama, please be guided accordingly!"[n] Badlands analyst Burning Bright wrote that the canal deployment tracked the same memetic and media structure as Trump's Canada messaging, using the same templates, and had succeeded in pushing global discussion toward the [[monroe-doctrine|Monroe Doctrine]] and the Panama Papers.[n]
December 2024 Remarks on Ukraine's Church and Russia's Past Leaders

At his end-of-year press conference in December 2024, Putin said the largest Christian church in Ukraine was being persecuted because the country is run by godless people, and that Ukrainian leader [[volodymyr-zelensky|Vladimir Zelensky]] and many of his associates are "ethnic Jews" who have never been seen at a synagogue.[n] He described Zelensky's earlier outlawing of the [[ukrainian-orthodox-church|Ukrainian Orthodox Church]] over alleged links to Moscow as a "blatant violation of human rights, the rights of believers," adding that "the church is being torn apart in front of the whole world. It is like an execution by a firing squad."[n] He predicted the crackdown would come back to haunt Zelensky's government, and said its members were not even atheists: "Atheists are people who believe in something, they believe… that there is no God. But it is their faith, their conviction. But these people are not atheists. These are simply people without any faith at all, infidels."[n]

In a separate interview published by Russia 1 TV journalist Pavel Zarubin on Telegram, Putin said Russia would never sacrifice its national interests to improve relations with any nation or bloc, and accused a previous generation of Russian politicians of having "gone so far as to destroy their own country in hope that Russia will become a part of the so-called 'civilized world'" led by Washington and its allies — achieving nothing, because the West never intended to accept Russia as an equal.[n] The remarks referred to the post-Soviet period, when Russia's shift from a command economy to capitalism produced a deep crisis, ruble devaluation, and the 1998 debt default widely regarded as the worst economic crisis in the nation's modern history.[n] Badlands commentator GhostofBasedPatrickHenry linked the remarks to Revelation 2:9 and its "synagogue of Satan" passage addressed to the church at Smyrna, and asked whether Putin's "ethnic Jews" meant Ashkenazi Jews or the [[khazaria|Khazars]] — noting Putin's own Tucker Carlson history lesson about Rurik, Sviatoslav I's defeat of Khazaria in 965, and Vladimir the Great's baptism at Sevastopol in 988.[n]

At his December 2024 end-of-year press conference, Russian President [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] said Zelensky and many of his associates are "ethnic Jews" who have never been seen at a synagogue, and characterized Ukraine as being run by godless people without any faith at all.[n] Putin condemned Zelensky's outlawing of the [[ukrainian-orthodox-church|Ukrainian Orthodox Church]] earlier that year over alleged links to Moscow as a "blatant violation of human rights, the rights of believers," comparing the church's treatment to "an execution by a firing squad," and said he was certain the crackdown would come back to haunt members of Zelensky's government.[n]
Putin's December 2024 Defense of the Church

The Ukrainian Orthodox Church (UOC), described by RT as the largest Christian church in Ukraine, was outlawed by [[volodymyr-zelensky|Vladimir Zelensky]] in 2024 over alleged links to Moscow.[n] At his end-of-year press conference that December, Russian President [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] called the ban a "blatant violation of human rights, the rights of believers," saying "the church is being torn apart in front of the whole world. It is like an execution by a firing squad."[n] He attributed the persecution to a Ukrainian leadership he described as faithless infidels rather than atheists, and predicted the crackdown would come back to haunt them.[n]
Campaign for Federal Death Row Commutations

Amnesty International led a weeks-long push, joined by other NGOs, pressuring President [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] to commute the sentences of all prisoners on federal and military death rows ahead of the end of his term.[n] Part of the campaign's argument was that the death penalty is applied in a racially discriminatory way, citing figures that of 460 federal defendants who faced the death penalty, 119 were white and 341 came from minority groups, including 237 Black defendants.[n] On December 23, 2024, Biden commuted 37 of the 40 federal death sentences, an action documented at [[2024-federal-death-row-commutations]].[n]

A December 20, 2024 report from the global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas found that 1,991 CEOs had departed U.S. companies as of November — "the highest total on record."[n] The report noted the figure "has surpassed the previous record of 1,914 CEO exits that occurred in all of 2023" and was up 16 percent from the 1,710 exits during the same period the prior year.[n] Interim replacements rose from seven percent of CEO successions in 2023 to 13 percent in 2024.[n] Senior Vice President Andrew Challenger said, "The current landscape has a lot of uncertainty baked in, and companies are responding by putting temporary leaders in place. This can act as a trial run to see how the leader navigates current challenges," adding that "it's much less disruptive to replace an interim head if things do not appear to be working out, not only [for] the company and its employees, but also to analysts and shareholders."[n] The government/non-profit sector recorded the most departures year-to-date at 438, followed by health care/products, technology, entertainment/leisure, financial, services, and hospitals; California led the states with 223 departures, followed by New York, Texas, and Florida.[n] Common stated reasons included retirement, pursuing new opportunities, and transitioning to a different role within the same company, while Challenger had earlier suggested in September that economic changes were a key driver.[n] Badlands analyst Burning Bright cited Intel, Boeing, and Stellantis and remarked that it was strange for "progenitors of the System" to be "dropping like flies while the System is 'in control.'"[n]

The [[house-ethics-committee|House Ethics Committee]] released its report into Gaetz's past conduct on December 23, 2024, after he filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block its publication.[n] The report said investigators found "substantial evidence" that the former congressman violated House rules, Florida state laws, and federal laws, alleging he paid tens of thousands of dollars to women for drugs or sex in at least 20 instances, including paying a 17-year-old girl for sex in 2017.[n] Panel investigators wrote that there was substantial evidence Gaetz "violated House Rules and other standards of conduct prohibiting prostitution, statutory rape, illicit drug use, impermissible gifts, special favors or privileges, and obstruction of Congress."[n] Having resigned from Congress the previous month after being nominated by President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] for U.S. attorney general, Gaetz argued in his suit — filed in federal court in Washington and naming the committee and its chair, Rep. [[michael-guest|Michael Guest]], as defendants — that the panel lacked jurisdiction over him as a private citizen and that the report contained "untruthful and defamatory information" that could "significantly damage" his standing and reputation.[n] His attorneys called the release "an unprecedented overreach that threatens fundamental constitutional rights and established procedural protections."[n] Gaetz subsequently released evidence he said refuted the report.[n]

On December 23, 2024, the committee released its report into the conduct of former Rep. [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] (R-Fla.), hours after he filed a federal lawsuit seeking an emergency order to block publication.[n] The report concluded there was "substantial evidence" that Gaetz violated House rules, Florida state laws, and federal laws, including allegations that he paid tens of thousands of dollars to women for drugs or sex in at least 20 instances and paid a 17-year-old girl for sex in 2017.[n] Gaetz's suit named the committee and its chair, Rep. [[michael-guest|Michael Guest]] (R-Miss.), as defendants and argued that the panel had exceeded its constitutional authority by acting against a former member and had failed to observe due process and its own procedural rules.[n]

As chair of the [[house-ethics-committee|House Ethics Committee]], Rep. Michael Guest (R-Miss.) was named as a defendant, alongside the committee itself, in the federal lawsuit former Rep. [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] filed on December 23, 2024 in an attempt to block release of the committee's report into his conduct.[n] The committee published the report the same day.[n]

Following the December 2024 investor lawsuit against the team behind the [[hawk-memecoin|$HAWK]] token tied to [[haliey-welch|Haliey Welch]], Badlands commentator Ashe in America argued that regulators would seize on the high-profile collapse to expand oversight of crypto markets, writing that the SEC "has been flirting with shitcoins for a while" and appeared poised to finally act.[n] The suit itself alleged that HAWK functioned as an unregistered security under established legal precedent.[n]

Post-mortem research conducted after the party's sweeping 2024 losses found deeper problems than the candidacies of [[kamala-harris|Kamala Harris]] or [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]].[n] In a trio of focus groups run by the progressive group [[navigator-research|Navigator Research]] and shared first with [[politico|Politico]], even voters who had previously backed Democrats described the party as weak and overly focused on diversity and elites.[n] Asked to compare the party to an animal, one participant chose an ostrich with "their heads in the sand," another chose koalas who are "complacent and lazy about getting policy wins," and a third said Democrats are "not a friend of the working class anymore."[n] Rachael Russell, Navigator's director of polling and analytics, called the results "a pretty scathing rebuke" of the Democratic Party brand.[n] With no clear party leader and losses across nearly every demographic, Democrats entered a second Trump presidency without a unified strategy, while internal blame was variously assigned to Biden, inflation, and "losing hold of culture."[n]
Politico Analysis of the Annulled Romanian Election

A December 2024 Politico analysis framed Georgescu's rise as a victory for [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]], noting that residents of Mihail Kogălniceanu — a town on Romania's Black Sea coast beside a NATO airstrip being expanded into the alliance's largest base in Europe, slated to host some 10,000 military personnel by 2030 — voted overwhelmingly for him.[n] The anti-Brussels, NATO-skeptic ultranationalist emerged seemingly from nowhere to seize pole position in the election's first round, sending Romania's establishment into a crisis of confidence.[n] After incumbent President [[klaus-iohannis|Klaus Iohannis]] released secret files alleging the vote had been compromised by a likely Russia-backed "hybrid" attack and a vast TikTok influence operation, Romania's Constitutional Court canceled the entire election.[n]

As incumbent Romanian president in late 2024, Iohannis released secret files alleging that the presidential vote won in the first round by [[calin-georgescu|Călin Georgescu]] had been compromised by a likely Russia-backed "hybrid" attack and a vast TikTok influence operation.[n] Romania's Constitutional Court subsequently canceled the entire election.[n]

Badlands commentary in December 2024 noted that the NSA is one of several notable organizations headquartered at [[fort-meade|Fort Meade]], Maryland, alongside the combatant command [[us-cyber-command|CYBERCOM]], the Military Intelligence Civilian Excepted Career Program, the [[defense-information-systems-agency|Defense Information Systems Agency]], the [[defense-information-school|Defense Information School]], and the [[defense-media-activity|Defense Media Activity]] — the same installation that hosted [[project-stargate|Project Stargate]].[n]
Fort Meade and the Devolution Thesis

In a December 2024 Badlands News Brief, GhostofBasedPatrickHenry observed that CYBERCOM is a combatant command based at [[fort-meade|Fort Meade]], Maryland — the same installation that hosted [[project-stargate|Project Stargate]] and houses the [[national-security-agency|NSA]] — and noted that CYBERCOM "plays a starring role in Jon Herold's Devolution series."[n]
